healthContext: Alexander reports nothing of his own body; his only health observation concerns a comrade, Thos. Small, who lost a leg at Ringgold and was "doing well and seemed very cheerful" in Nashville hospital No. 8 — a hopeful note on amputation recovery. His collective "All the boys from Champlain are well" is a third-person group reassurance, not a statement about his own condition.

No content on the author's own health. He notes the Chickamauga dead buried opposite camp, men who "died from the effects of their wounds" at the general hospital — a reminder of how many wounds proved mortal through later infection rather than on the field.

Charles affirms good health after the multi-day sea voyage on the steamship Mississippi from Alexandria to New Orleans, explicitly denying seasickness despite rough weather and crowded, four-or-five-to-a-bunk holds. The denial of cold suffering and seasickness reads as genuine rather than merely formulaic.

Charles is judged fit enough that the Lieut. Col. "could not spare so healthy a man" from clerk detail, and he calls his own health "pretty good." One ambiguity: when asked if he could stand a long march, he answered no — possibly modesty about his preference for the desk, possibly a mild reservation about endurance, but no ailment is named.
The image of an "ancient philosopher" falling into a ditch and breaking his neck is a playful hypothetical warning against flattery, not a report of any real injury to the author.

Charles affirms "very good" health from his New Orleans desk post, well removed from the field, framing it reassuringly ("I hope you don't worry about us boys"). The woman killed by the streetcar is an accidental civilian death, unrelated to the author's wellness.
Charles affirms good health in his comfortable third-story clerk billet at New Orleans headquarters; no ailment, the statement consistent with his described easy, well-fed circumstances.
Alexander's "very anxious" feeling concerns the silence from home, not any physical complaint of his own.

Alexander writes of camp amusements in good spirits but confesses "I feel quite sad tonight" ("the blues"), a transient low mood he himself flags as melancholy rather than illness; too general to read as homesickness, and no physical ailment is reported.
No content on the author's own health. He fears his mother may be "sick" (her, not him) and reports a fellow clerk's fatal drunken fall — an accidental death, not disease.

Alexander reports nothing of his own body. He pities six fresh Indiana regiments arriving "poor and haggard — worn out" who "left large numbers on the way unable to march" — a vivid picture of how hard marching broke down unseasoned troops, but concerning others, not the author.

Charles's "I will be there to help, if not sick" is a conditional about a possible future, not a current ailment. He asks after Alex's health and recounts the fellow clerk's fatal drunken fall over a third-story rail — an accidental death, not the author's own condition.

On the eve of marching to the front, Alexander braces his mother for the possibility of death in the coming "death struggle," but this is anticipatory and spiritual, not a report of any present physical ailment.
